title: Section check: War, independence and rebuilding
intro: 6 questions about Lessons 7–9. Take your time. You can look back at the lessons and try again as often as you like.

questions.question: What happened in Singapore on 15 February 1942?

options.text: The occupation came to an end.
options.feedback: Not quite. The occupation ended in 1945. On 15 February 1942, it began. Look back at Lesson 7.
Not quite. In 1942, Japanese lessons became compulsory in schools. Look back at Lesson 7.
Yes. British forces gave up at the Ford Factory. Then the occupation began. It lasted until 1945.

questions.question: You want to learn what people in Singapore ate in 1943. Which source would help most?

options.feedback: Yes. Lee Geok Boi used oral history interviews to write about food in this time. Memories can tell us about meals.

options.text: A 2025 photo of the Former Ford Factory
options.feedback: Not quite. The photo shows the building in 2025. It cannot show what people ate in 1943. Look back at Lesson 7.
Not quite. That rule tells us about school lessons, not meals. Look back at Lesson 7.

questions.question: On 17 August 1945, two leaders said in public that Indonesia was free. What is this kind of statement called?

options.feedback: Yes. A proclamation is a statement made to all. In Indonesia, people mark 17 August as the day they became free.
Not quite. The Netherlands handed over power later, in 1949. That came after the proclamation. Look back at Lesson 8.
Not quite. A federation is a group of states joined under one main government. Look back at Lesson 8.

questions.question: A student says that Malaysia became free on 31 August 1957. What needs to change?

options.feedback: Not quite. 17 August 1945 is the date of Indonesia's proclamation. Look back at Lesson 8.

options.text: Change Malaysia to the Federation of Malaya
options.feedback: Yes. It was the Federation of Malaya that became free in 1957. Malaysia was formed later, in 1963.
Not quite. In 1956, leaders signed an agreement in London. It set the day of independence in 1957. Look back at Lesson 8.

questions.question: In March 2000, a UN report said many schools in Timor-Leste had been repaired. What does this date tell you?

options.feedback: Not quite. The report is from 2000. That is before independence was restored in 2002. Look back at Lesson 9.
Yes. Work on schools began before 2002, while a UN team ran the country with East Timorese leaders.
Not quite. 2024 is the date of the school photo. Repairs began much earlier. Look back at Lesson 9.

stimulus.title: A made-up school in a made-up town
stimulus.body: This is a made-up example. The made-up town of Lorvan has a new school building with a strong roof. But there are very few books. Most teachers have had no training. Many children do not understand the language used in class.

questions.question: What would help the children in Lorvan learn the most?

options.text: New paint on the school walls
options.feedback: Not quite. The building is already fixed. A school needs more than walls. Look back at Lesson 9.

options.text: A big party to open the school
options.feedback: Not quite. A party lasts one day. Learning needs teachers, books and a language children know. Look back at Lesson 9.

options.text: Teachers, books and a known language
options.feedback: Yes. In Timor-Leste, too, buildings were fixed first. Teachers, books and language are also needed for learning.

results.high: Well done. You kept the dates in order, and you saw what each source can show.
results.middle: Good work. You got many questions right. Look back at the lessons for the ones you missed, and try again if you like.
results.low: Thank you for trying. Look back at Lessons 7–9, then try again. You can take as long as you need.
